January. Ana and Mihai are in the kitchen writing their resolutions for the new year on a sheet stuck to the fridge. Elena, after the scare in December, has suddenly become very health-conscious.

And she says she still hasn’t got used to it. That coffee without sugar tastes like a punishment.

SWEH-lo (present, “ue” diphthong), so-LEE-a (imperfect, no diphthong). Like poder: puedo / podía.
a-kos-toom-BRAR-seh: a long word, stress on BRAR.
pro-PO-see-to: stress on the second syllable, written with an accent.
“Soler” expresses a HABIT. It’s only used in the present and the imperfect, always followed by an infinitive. It’s conjugated like “poder” (o → ue):
Suelo caminar cada día. (I usually walk)
Solía fumar. (I used to smoke — not any more)
“Solía + infinitive” is like English “used to” and an elegant alternative to the plain imperfect: «De niño solía ir al pueblo» = «De niño iba al pueblo».
2. Acostumbrarse a vs estar acostumbrado a
Ya se acostumbrará al café solo.
No está acostumbrada a comer sin sal.
Both take the preposition A + noun or infinitive (where English uses -ing: used to eating). With a clause: acostumbrarse a que + subjunctive: «No me acostumbro a que me llamen señora».
“Acostumbrar a + infinitive” (without se) = to be in the habit of doing something, a formal synonym of soler: «Acostumbra a cenar temprano».

“Seguir” is used with the GERUND, not the infinitive: «Sigue fumando», not «sigue a fumar». Negative: «Sigue sin fumar» = He still doesn’t smoke.

It all started one Tuesday in December, at Obor market. Elena had been going there every Tuesday and every Friday for forty years, always at the same time, always to the same stalls. She knew all the stallholders by name, and they knew her.

That Tuesday, as she was choosing some apples at Mr Nelu’s stall, she suddenly felt the ground move. The apples went blurry. It seemed to her that the noise of the market was fading away, as if someone had turned down the volume of the world.
The next thing she remembered was Mr Nelu’s face, very close to hers, and a woman she didn’t know putting a coat under her head. She was on the ground, among crates of apples.
“Mrs Elena, can you hear me?” the stallholder kept saying. “Someone call an ambulance!”

Ana was teaching when her phone rang. It was an unknown number. She didn’t usually answer during class, but something told her she had to this time. It was Mr Nelu, who had found her number in Elena’s phone under the name “Ana — daughter-in-law”.
Twenty minutes later, Ana and Mihai rushed into A&E. Elena was lying on a stretcher, pale but awake, with a drip in her arm and a far from friendly expression.
“It’s nothing,” she said as soon as she saw them. “A dizzy spell. These people are exaggerating. I want to go home, I’ve left the sarmale half-made.”

But it wasn’t “nothing”. The blood tests showed her blood sugar was very high, well above normal. The doctor, a young woman with glasses and infinite patience, explained that Elena had type two diabetes, probably for years, without knowing it. The dizzy spell had been a warning.
“It isn’t serious if it’s kept under control,” said the doctor. “But you need to change some of your habits. Do you usually eat sweets?”
Elena looked at Mihai. Mihai looked at the ceiling. Ana bit her lip.

Mihai coughed. In his mother’s house there was always, without exception, a tray of cozonac, a tray of pastries, a jar of cherry preserve and a box of chocolates hidden in the cupboard “for guests”. Guests came once a month. The box was emptied every week.

The doctor gave her a long list. She recommended that she give up sugar and sweets, eat less white bread and more vegetables, walk at least half an hour a day and repeat the tests in three months. She also gave her a prescription for a medicine she had to take every morning.
Elena listened in silence. When the doctor had finished, she asked just one thing:
The doctor smiled. “One small piece. Just one. On Christmas Day.”
Elena sighed as if a sentence had been read out to her.

The first days were very hard. Elena wasn’t used to living without sugar. Coffee tasted bitter to her, tea tasted like dirty water, and wholemeal bread was “horse food”. She got angry about everything. Twice Mihai found her in the kitchen at night, looking sadly at the box of chocolates.

In the end it was Rosa Elena who saved her, without knowing it. The little girl had just learned to ride a bike and wanted to go to the park every day. So Elena started taking her every afternoon at four, to Ioanid Park. At first they did one lap. Then two. By the third week they were doing four laps, and Elena no longer got tired.

In the park she met other grandmothers. One of them, Mrs Florica, had had diabetes for ten years and gave her all her tricks: cozonac with honey instead of sugar, walnuts instead of sweets, cinnamon in coffee so it isn’t so bitter.
“At first you think you’ll never get used to it,” Florica told her. “But one day you realise you don’t miss it any more. And on top of that, you feel much better.”
She was right. By the end of December, Elena was sleeping better, had more energy and had lost three kilos. And most surprising of all: she had stopped complaining. Well, almost.

It coincided with the end of the club’s challenge: a month without plastic. On the last Friday of the year, all the members gathered at Ana and Mihai’s for a dinner where everyone had to share their experience.

Costel said he had stopped buying water in plastic bottles and now had a glass demijohn in his lorry. Mr Dan admitted he had failed completely, because his wife kept buying everything wrapped, but at least he had learned to recycle. Mrs Ecaterina said she hadn’t had to change anything, because she still lived as if it were 1970.
When it was Elena’s turn, everyone expected her to talk about plastic. But she stood up, went to the kitchen and came back with a tray.
“This month I learned two things,” she said, and Ana translated. “First, that you can live without plastic bags. Second, that you can live without sugar. The second is harder.”
On the tray was a cozonac. But it was a different cozonac: darker, flatter, with walnuts from the market and honey from her village.
“Sugar-free,” she announced. “My friend Florica’s recipe. If you don’t like it, tell me, I won’t be offended. Well, a little bit.”
They all tasted it somewhat suspiciously. Costel was the first to speak, with his mouth full.
“Mrs Elena, if you hadn’t told me, I wouldn’t have noticed. It’s very good.”
Elena looked at him suspiciously, searching his face for a lie. But Costel was already taking a second slice, and Mr Dan a third. In ten minutes the tray was empty.

That night, after everyone had left, Ana found Elena in the kitchen, in front of the cupboard again. But this time she wasn’t looking at the box of chocolates. She was putting it into a cloth bag to give to the neighbours.
“I don’t need it any more,” she said, without turning round. “And besides, Vasile’s walnut tree needs me to be here in ten years to eat its walnuts. I promised Ileana.”

They spent New Year’s Eve at home, the four of them, with Aunt Viorica connected by video call from her flat in the centre. At five to twelve, Viorica asked to see the garden. Mihai went out with the phone and pointed it towards the bottom of the garden, where the little walnut tree, covered in snow, looked like a stick stuck in a white cake.
“It’s still alive,” said Viorica, bringing her face very close to the screen. “Walnut trees are stubborn. Like the people in this family.”

When the bells rang, everyone said their main resolution out loud. Mihai: to start running again. Ana: to sleep more. Viorica: to learn to use her phone without anyone helping her. And Elena, after thinking for a long time, said:
“I want to keep walking. All the way to Kyoto, if necessary.”

They all laughed, but Ana kept thinking about that sentence. In the summer, Mihai’s contract at the hospital would end; it had already been extended once. In a few months they would have to decide what to do: stay, go back to Madrid or start something new somewhere else. Until now they had avoided talking about it. But looking at Elena, at Viorica, at the walnut tree under the snow and at her daughter asleep on the sofa, with the paper crane printed on her pyjamas, Ana felt the decision wasn’t going to be as easy as they had thought when they came.
Outside, in the garden, the snow kept falling slowly on the old stump and the new tree, making no distinction between them.

Ana turned off the living-room light, covered her daughter with a blanket and, for the first time in months, left the marking unfinished on the table. It was ten past twelve. The deal was off to a good start.

Cozonac sin azúcar de doamna Florica
Ingredients: a kilo of flour, six eggs, half a litre of milk, a hundred grams of butter, two hundred grams of honey and three hundred grams of walnuts.
I usually start the night before: I leave the yeast with a little warm milk so it’s ready in the morning.
